title: A Linux calendar panel from a PF1007L photo frame
job: Check the exact frame and plan an experimental microSD Linux dashboard without confusing board variants.
description: Plan a source-backed PF1007L Linux dashboard: identify the tested Allwinner variant, preserve recovery, and understand the limits before writing a spare card.

sources.label: Pinned Omarchy frame README and evidence limits
PF1007L identity and original Android paths

bodyHtml:
Not hardware-tested by Hackshop

This is a source-checked planning guide. Author reports, simulations and our original diagrams are not independent physical verification. No purchase, device modification or account connection is performed by this page.

The Omarchy frame project documents a Linux web-view route for the Humblestead HM-PF1007-BK / EFERCRO PF1007L with an Allwinner A33. It is a specific experimental target, not a universal photo-frame image. The existing Android route remains a separate option.

Before a write

  1. Identify, do not infer from the listing. Compare the board and display, touch and radio components with the pinned README. Rockchip BIUFRAME instructions do not apply. Unknown identity means stop.
  2. Preserve recovery. Keep the original card, a verified backup and a separate blank microSD. Read the restore guide first. Do not overwrite internal eMMC or copy a sample disk identifier.
  3. Use the correct inputs. The build needs the matching proprietary touch firmware from the owner's original backup. It is not included in Git. Preserve private keys, device identifiers and backups outside public repositories.
  4. Make a separate write decision. Inspect the project writer's checks, the exact removable disk and its byte count before approving a card write. Never alter guards to make an unknown unit pass.

Prove the base before the dashboard

Follow the pinned project's sequence for recovery access and the usable boot label before desktop provisioning. The source distinguishes an author-reported working installation from an original image-builder run validated in QEMU. A fresh image still needs testing on the exact frame. A successful build or emulator boot does not prove its display or recovery path.

A useful first design

Start with one read-only calendar or household status page. Use large text, a last-updated time and an offline state. Test readability, touch, wake, reboot and recovery before mounting it. Add power, a card and mounting to the budget; no current compatible seller price is verified here. Keep remote-AI credentials on a trusted backend. Local dictation in the source uses audio from a Mac, not a verified built-in microphone.

Walkthrough status

No Hackshop real-device video or finished-build photo is available. A future walkthrough should show the exact board, a cold boot, an actual calendar update and recovery. This diagram is not that footage.

title: Plan House Control with Hue and Home Assistant
job: Connect a 3D home interface without confusing simulation, cloud integrations and physical proof.
description: A source-checked House Control setup path with Hue, Home Assistant, simulated-device boundaries and limited AI access.

sources.label: Pinned House Control implementation and MIT license notice
Pinned device connections and Apple Home limitations
Pinned AI Access permissions and privacy

bodyHtml:
Not hardware-tested by Hackshop

This is a source-checked planning guide. Author reports, simulations and our original diagrams are not independent physical verification. No purchase, device modification or account connection is performed by this page.

House Control now has an inspectable implementation behind its apartment-style 3D interface. The scene is not proof that a particular lamp or air conditioner works. Treat it as an interface connected through explicitly chosen integrations, not a universal device exploit.

Start without connecting a home

  1. Review the pinned version. Follow its build or release verification instructions on a suitable Mac or iPhone. Do not disable platform security checks merely because a guide contains a shortcut.
  2. Explore the demo plan. Leave real accounts disconnected. Unlinked devices are simulated. Use this mode to decide how rooms, scenes and controls should look.
  3. Choose one low-risk lamp. The Hue route uses a local bridge; Home Assistant uses your server's API. Smart Life uses Tuya's cloud and differs between app editions. Keep these routes distinct.
  4. Pair deliberately. Use the project's connection guide and keep credentials private. Never paste a real home token or private link into a public issue or tutorial.
  5. Verify both directions. Toggle the lamp, inspect the real light and check state after changing it through its normal control. A moving render alone proves only the UI changed. Keep exact models and test results in your own notes.

Compatibility is per route

The source says Apple Home devices are controlled on iPhone; on Mac that route is linking/simulated, not equivalent local control. Supported platforms do not establish support for every appliance model. Leave climate control out of the first experiment and retain the normal physical controls.

Optional agent access

Keep AI Access off for initial setup. Its private link carries access for whoever has it. If later enabled, start read-only, restrict permissions, select a short expiry and stop the link when finished. The AI provider may see room names, device state and the floor plan; a tunnel is not a promise that nobody else handles the traffic. This guide neither opens a tunnel nor controls your devices.

Walkthrough status

No Hackshop hardware-control video or finished-build photo is available. A demo-plan screen recording can illustrate navigation only. A physical walkthrough must visibly show the linked lamp and its state changing; request permission before reusing maker footage.

title: Read an old Siri Remote's events on Linux
job: Plan the documented A1962 event-reader path without promising unverified keyboard or voice features.
description: Reuse a gen-1 A1962 Siri Remote as a source-documented Linux event reader, with model, permission and reconnect limitations.

sources.label: Pinned implementation, test scope and MIT license notice
Pinned measured, reported and guessed protocol observations
Pinned device-access rules and optional input permission

bodyHtml:
Not hardware-tested by Hackshop

This is a source-checked planning guide. Author reports, simulations and our original diagrams are not independent physical verification. No purchase, device modification or account connection is performed by this page.

The open-appleremote project reports finding, unlocking and reading an A1962 first-generation Siri Remote on Linux. An A1513 is expected to work but remains untested in the pinned README. Newer Siri Remotes and the older infrared Apple Remote are not interchangeable targets.

A bounded first session

  1. Check model and host. Compare the exact remote and Linux/BlueZ requirements with the pinned README. Confirm that an owned remote can be unpaired or removed from the host afterward.
  2. Inspect before running. Review the repository, then follow its pairing instructions. A Bluetooth connection alone does not prove decoded input; the project describes an unlock step for each connection.
  3. Grant narrow access. Start with the documented hidraw access for the logged-in user. Do not enable the optional virtual-input rule just to watch events. That extra permission allows programs to inject keystrokes.
  4. Observe, then test reconnect. Read button and touch events before mapping any action. Compare a deliberate button press with the reported event, then test sleep and reconnect. Avoid logging the remote's serial-number name or other devices' identifiers.

Button map, not a promised keyboard

The source names Menu, TV/Home, Play/Pause, volume, Siri and touch/click inputs. Map a harmless action only after observation. The optional keyboard path is not hardware-tested according to the README. Voice is unreleased and replay/synthetic-tested in this package; illustrative voice commands are not evidence of a working voice assistant.

Reconnect and privacy

The documented reconnect workaround disables LE privacy on the host. That changes behavior beyond this one application: assess it rather than making it an automatic setup step. Raw Bluetooth captures may include sensitive traffic and voice. Do not publish them. Use the project's non-audio sample to understand event shapes, with replay clearly labeled.

Walkthrough status

No Hackshop real-device recording or finished-build photo is available. A replay demonstration would show the decoder, not a live remote. A future physical walkthrough should show the exact A1962, button-to-event correspondence and sleep/reconnect. Current used-device pricing is unknown.
